title: Grade 4 HINDU RELIGIOUS EDUCATION — 4.1 Dainik Prarthana (Daily prayers)

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Dainik Prarthana means daily prayer. This sub-strand teaches three Sanatan prayers: the Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey, and Saraswati Vandana. You will learn when each is recited, what the words mean, and how to behave in a Hindu mandir, including mandirs in Kenya.

## Strand 4.0: Worship
Sub-strand 4.1: Dainik Prarthana (Daily prayers)
Suggested lessons: 10

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation
b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith
c) appreciate the importance of prayers in daily life for spiritual development
d) identify the Hindu places of worship in their locality for familiarisation
e) map the Hindu Mandir (temples) in Kenya for exact location
f) observe rites and rituals while visiting Sanatan/Hindu Mandirs in Kenya (temple)
g) appreciate the architecture of the place of worship for developing a sense of aesthetics

## What this sub-strand covers
• Gayatri Mantra
• Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey
• Saraswati Vandana

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why are prayers important in our daily life?
2. What is the significance of reciting prayers at different times?
3. Why are rites and rituals observed in a Sanatan/Hindu Mandir?

## Core competencies
• Communication: Learner develops speaking skills during practice of reciting prayers with peers.
• Digital Literacy: Learner interacts with technology by using search engines for enhancing information about Sanatan/Hindu Mandir.

## Values
• Respect: Learner inculcates humility during practice of reciting prayers with peers.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Citizenship: Learner enhances social cohesion when visiting Sanatan/Hindu Mandir (temple) to witness the rites and rituals, architecture and important features of the Sanatan/Hindu Mandir (temple).

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link the skill of applying geographical knowledge and using digital devices to map the Sanatan/Hindu Mandir (temple) in Kenya to skills learnt in Social Studies.
• Learner is able to link skills of making collage of pictures of temples in their locality a draw and colour the Sanatan/Hindu Mandir (temple) to the creative skills learnt in Creative Arts.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 4.0 Worship, Sub-strand 4.1 Dainik Prarthana (Daily prayers)

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Why daily prayer matters

LESSON 1: WHY DAILY PRAYER MATTERS
==================================

## What you will learn
• Explain why prayer is part of a day, not only of a festival.
• Name the three prayers to be learned and a time that fits each one.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; c) appreciate the importance of prayers in daily life for spiritual development

## Introduction
Some people only fold their hands when they are afraid. Daily prayer is steadier than that. It is a way of beginning the morning, starting study, or ending worship by remembering God on purpose.

## Notes
### What prayer is
Prayer is speaking with Paramatma. It can be thanks, praise, a request for a clean mind, or a promise to do what is right. In Sanatan life, set prayers are learned by heart so that the mouth and the mind can rest on true words instead of rushing into the day.

Daily prayer does not replace kindness. A learner who chants and then cheats has missed the point. Prayer is meant to make the rest of the day more honest, more attentive and less selfish. That is spiritual development: a slow growth in love of God and in good character.

### Three prayers, different moments
This sub-strand names three prayers, all from Sanatan or Hindu tradition:
- **Gayatri Mantra** — a morning and worship prayer asking the divine light to guide the mind
- **Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey** — a prayer of trust, often near the close of worship, saying that God is mother, father, friend and everything
- **Saraswati Vandana** — a salutation to Saraswati before study, asking for true learning

Knowing which prayer fits which occasion is part of familiarisation. You would not treat a prayer before study as a joke at the back of the class, and you would not rush the Gayatri while pushing in a queue.

### Times of day
Morning prayer sets the mind before work. A prayer before lessons asks for understanding rather than for an easy way to avoid work. An evening or closing prayer hands the day back to God, including the parts that went badly. Festivals have extra prayers, but these three are for ordinary days.

Recite only the words you have been taught carefully. Do not invent extra lines. Listen to a correct recording if your teacher provides one, and match the sound with respect.

## Key words
• dainik — daily
• prarthana — prayer
• familiarisation — getting to know something so that it is no longer strange

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which prayer fits the start of a study period: Saraswati Vandana, a made-up rhyme, or a joke about a classmate?

Working:
1. Saraswati is honoured as the deity of learning.
2. Saraswati Vandana is the prayer this sub-strand links with study.
3. A joke is not a prayer.

Answer: Saraswati Vandana.

## Activity: Prayers and occasions
You will need: Three cards, A resource person or teacher
1. Listen as a resource person or teacher names the three prayers and one occasion for each.
2. Label the cards Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey and Saraswati Vandana.
3. Under each title write the occasion: guiding the mind, trusting God as parent and friend, or beginning study.
4. Say why a daily prayer can help a learner more than praying only in a panic.

## Practice
1. What does Dainik Prarthana mean?
2. Name the three prayers in this sub-strand.
3. Why is prayer before an examination not a substitute for revision?

## Summary
• Daily prayer remembers God and steadies the day.
• The three prayers are the Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey and Saraswati Vandana.
• Each prayer has a fitting time.

### Answers to practice
1. Daily prayer.
2. Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey and Saraswati Vandana.
3. Prayer asks for a clear and honest mind. The learner still needs to study.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: The Gayatri Mantra

LESSON 2: THE GAYATRI MANTRA
============================

## What you will learn
• Recite the Gayatri Mantra correctly and calmly.
• Explain its meaning in simple English.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith

## Introduction
The Gayatri Mantra is a very old Vedic prayer to the divine light that gives understanding. Many Sanatan families recite it in the morning. You will learn the words slowly, then the meaning, so that the mouth does not run ahead of the mind.

## Notes
### The words
Learn this form, line by line:

Om bhur bhuvah svah
Tat savitur varenyam
Bhargo devasya dhimahi
Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat

Say it softly at first. Keep the ends of the words clear. Do not turn it into a race. If a line is difficult, your teacher or a recording can give the sound. Intonation means the rise and fall of the voice. A respectful tone is steady, not shouted and not giggled.

### The meaning
In simple English the prayer says: we meditate on the excellent glory of the Creator, the divine light. May that light inspire and guide our understanding.

Bhur, bhuvah and svah name the earth, the middle space and the heaven, a way of saying the whole world. Savitur points to the divine source of light. The last line is the request: may our thoughts be led in the right direction.

### When it is used
The Gayatri is recited in the morning, at sandhya time in homes that keep that custom, and during many acts of worship. At school it may be recited at assembly when the teacher has chosen it. It is a prayer for wisdom, so it also fits a quiet moment before study. It is not a spell for winning by cheating.

### How to practise
Stand or sit straight. Hands may be joined. Breathe in, then recite without straining the throat. Learn one line a day if you need to. When you can say all four lines, add the meaning in your own words so that faith and understanding stay together.

All learners in the class may learn this prayer as part of the lesson. Reciting it is a way of understanding Sanatan worship. Join with respect, even if your family also has other prayers at home.

## Key words
• Gayatri Mantra — a Vedic prayer asking divine light to guide the mind
• intonation — the musical rise and fall of the voice when reciting

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner can say the Gayatri quickly but cannot explain it. What should they add?

Working:
1. Correct sound matters, but the outcome also asks for meaning.
2. They should be able to say that the prayer meditates on divine light and asks that light to guide the mind.
3. Speed without meaning is not enough.

Answer: They should learn the simple meaning and recite more calmly.

## Activity: Practise the Gayatri with a partner
You will need: The four lines written clearly by the teacher, An audio recording if one is available
1. Listen to the teacher or to a recording of the Gayatri Mantra.
2. Repeat one line at a time with a partner, then say all four lines together.
3. Tell your partner the meaning in your own words.
4. Encourage a classmate who needs a slower pace. Do not laugh at a mistake; model the line again.

## Practice
1. Write the four lines of the Gayatri Mantra you were taught.
2. What does the Gayatri ask for?
3. Name one fitting time to recite the Gayatri.

## Summary
• The Gayatri asks divine light to guide our understanding.
• It is recited in the morning and in worship, calmly and clearly.
• Meaning and correct words belong together.

### Answers to practice
1. Om bhur bhuvah svah. Tat savitur varenyam. Bhargo devasya dhimahi. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat.
2. That the divine light of the Creator will guide and inspire our minds.
3. In the morning, during worship, or quietly before study.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey

LESSON 3: TWAMEV MATA CHA PITA TWAMEY
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Recite Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey.
• Explain that the prayer calls God mother, father, friend and everything.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith

## Introduction
Children know what it is to need a parent or a friend. This prayer says that God is all of those, and more. It is a prayer of trust, often sung or spoken near the end of worship.

## Notes
### The words
The name on the design is Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey. The prayer is learned in these four lines:

Twameva mata cha pita twameva
Twameva bandhush cha sakha twameva
Twameva vidya dravinam twameva
Twameva sarvam mama deva deva

Twameva means 'you alone'. Speak the lines evenly. The sound 'cha' is 'and'. Do not skip the third line, which is easy to forget.

### The meaning
- You alone are my mother, and you alone are my father.
- You alone are my relative, and you alone are my friend.
- You alone are my knowledge, and you alone are my wealth.
- You alone are my everything, O God of gods.

The prayer does not tell you to ignore your human parents. It says that behind every good gift, including parents, friends and learning, is Paramatma. When a parent is far away, or a friend disappoints you, the prayer is a place to rest trust.

### When it is used
Many congregations recite it at the close of puja or aarti, when worshippers offer the whole day to God. It can also be a personal evening prayer. It is a prayer of belonging, not a prayer for showing off a loud voice.

### A meaning to keep
If God is your mother and father, then you are not abandoned. If God is your wealth, then cheating to get money is a strange answer to the prayer. If God is your knowledge, then learning is received with thanks, not with pride that insults slower learners.

Practise until you can recite it without the card, then say the meaning once in English.

## Key words
• twameva — you alone
• sakha — friend
• vidya — knowledge or learning

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which line means that God is mother and father, and which line means that God is knowledge and wealth?

Working:
1. Mata means mother and pita means father: the first line.
2. Vidya means knowledge and dravinam means wealth: the third line.
3. The second line is relative and friend. The fourth line says God is everything.

Answer: The first line is mother and father. The third line is knowledge and wealth.

## Activity: Recite and explain Twameva
You will need: The four lines on the board, Exercise book
1. Listen to the prayer from the teacher or an audio device.
2. Practise with a peer until both of you can say the four lines.
3. Write the English meaning of each line.
4. One pair recites during a class assembly or a class prayer time if the teacher invites you. Help a classmate who needs the lines pointed to as you say them.

## Practice
1. Recite the four lines of Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey.
2. What does the first line mean?
3. When is this prayer often recited?

## Summary
• Twameva says that God alone is mother, father, relative, friend, knowledge, wealth and everything.
• It is often recited at the close of worship.
• Trust in God should make us more grateful, not proud or dishonest.

### Answers to practice
1. Twameva mata cha pita twameva. Twameva bandhush cha sakha twameva. Twameva vidya dravinam twameva. Twameva sarvam mama deva deva.
2. You alone are my mother and you alone are my father.
3. At the close of puja or aarti, and as a prayer of trust.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Saraswati Vandana

LESSON 4: SARASWATI VANDANA
===========================

## What you will learn
• Recite the Saraswati Vandana used in this lesson.
• Explain who Saraswati is and why the prayer is said before study.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith

## Introduction
Before a music lesson or a page of reading, some learners simply start. A Sanatan prayer before study does something more. It greets Saraswati, the deity of knowledge, speech and the arts, and asks that learning be successful and clean.

## Notes
### Who Saraswati is
In Sanatan tradition Saraswati is the deity of learning, speech, music and wisdom. She is often shown in white, seated with a veena and a book, and with a swan nearby. White suggests a clear mind. The book suggests study. You do not need a picture in order to pray, but a picture can help you remember who is being greeted. A vandana is a salutation, a respectful greeting.

### The words to learn
This is the short vandana used before study:

Saraswati namastubhyam
Varade kamarupini
Vidyarambham karishyami
Siddhir bhavatu me sada

Namastubhyam means 'I bow to you'. Vidyarambham karishyami means 'I am about to begin my learning'. Siddhir bhavatu me sada means 'May success always be mine'.

The whole prayer says: O Saraswati, I bow to you, giver of blessings, who grants what is rightly wished. I am beginning my study. May I always succeed.

### Success of the right kind
Success here does not mean passing by copying. It means understanding, remembering and using knowledge well. A learner may recite this vandana at assembly, at the start of homework, or before a school performance of music or reading. Recite it, then do the work.

### Practice
Join your hands, recite slowly, and then open your book. If you forget a line, begin again rather than mumbling. Peers can test each other kindly: one says the first line, the other says the second, and then you swap.

## Key words
• Saraswati — the Sanatan deity of learning, speech and the arts
• vandana — a salutation or prayer of respectful greeting
• vidya — knowledge or learning

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A class wants a prayer for the moment they open their exercise books. Which of the three prayers fits best, and why?

Working:
1. The Gayatri asks for a guided mind and can also be used in the morning.
2. Twameva is especially a prayer of trust at the close of worship.
3. Saraswati Vandana directly says, 'I am beginning my learning.'

Answer: Saraswati Vandana, because it is a salutation before study.

## Activity: Saraswati Vandana before a short reading
You will need: The four lines on a chart, A paragraph of any school reading
1. Listen to the vandana and repeat each line.
2. Say the meaning together: I bow to Saraswati; I am beginning my learning; may I succeed.
3. Recite the prayer, then read one paragraph silently and tell a partner one fact you understood.
4. Invite a learner who speaks softly to recite with the group so that nobody is left out.

## Practice
1. Recite the Saraswati Vandana taught in this lesson.
2. Who is Saraswati?
3. What does 'Vidyarambham karishyami' mean?

## Summary
• Saraswati is the deity of learning.
• The vandana bows to her and asks for success as study begins.
• Real success includes honest work after the prayer.

### Answers to practice
1. Saraswati namastubhyam. Varade kamarupini. Vidyarambham karishyami. Siddhir bhavatu me sada.
2. The Sanatan deity of learning, speech, music and wisdom.
3. I am beginning my learning.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Reciting at the right time

LESSON 5: RECITING AT THE RIGHT TIME
====================================

## What you will learn
• Match each prayer to its occasion.
• Recite all three prayers with respect for classmates.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith; c) appreciate the importance of prayers in daily life for spiritual development

## Introduction
A tool used at the wrong time can still be a good tool. Prayer is similar. The words of the Gayatri, Twameva and the Saraswati Vandana are all valuable, and each one has a moment when its meaning is especially clear.

## Notes
### A simple guide
- Recite the **Gayatri Mantra** when you are beginning the day or joining worship and you want your mind led by divine light.
- Recite **Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey** when worship is closing or when you need to remember that God holds you as parent and friend.
- Recite **Saraswati Vandana** when you open a book, begin a lesson, or start music and art practice.

Nothing stops a family from using a prayer at another sincere moment. This guide stops the three from being jumbled in your memory.

### Why timing matters
Words sink in when they match the action. Saying 'I am beginning my learning' and then chatting for twenty minutes wastes the prayer. Saying 'you alone are my wealth' and then stealing a coin from a bag is a contradiction. The significance of time is that the body is about to do something, and the prayer points that action towards God.

### Manners while others recite
Stand still in assembly. If you are not reciting, keep silent rather than mocking the sound. Humility means you do not shove a partner who is slower. Offer the first line quietly if they ask for help. Correct intonation comes from listening, not from shouting over the group.

### A week's plan
Morning: Gayatri, even two careful repetitions. Before homework: Saraswati Vandana. After a family or class prayer: Twameva. At the end of the week, notice whether the prayers changed anything small: less panic, a kinder reply, or homework actually started.

Spiritual development is that noticing. The prayers are short enough for a child. Their meanings are large enough for a lifetime.

## Key words
• occasion — the time or event for which something is used
• humility — a modest spirit that does not put you above others

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Match the prayers to these moments: opening a mathematics book, morning assembly, the end of aarti.

Working:
1. Opening a book matches Saraswati Vandana.
2. Morning assembly matches the Gayatri Mantra.
3. The end of aarti matches Twameva.

Answer: Saraswati Vandana; Gayatri Mantra; Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey.

## Activity: Assembly practice
You will need: The three prayers written out, A quiet space
1. In pairs, recite each prayer once and say its occasion before you begin.
2. Listen to an audio recording if the teacher has one, and copy the calm pace.
3. As a class, recite one prayer as you would at assembly. Stand straight and wait for the signal to start.
4. Afterwards, tell your partner one reason daily prayer helps spiritual growth. Encourage a classmate who is still learning the lines.

## Practice
1. Which prayer is the best match for the start of homework, and why?
2. Give the meaning of Twameva in one sentence.
3. Why should you not mock a classmate who recites slowly?

## Summary
• Gayatri for morning and a guided mind, Saraswati Vandana before study, Twameva at the close of worship.
• The prayer should match the action that follows.
• Classmates recite together with humility.

### Answers to practice
1. Saraswati Vandana, because it greets the deity of learning as study begins.
2. You alone, O God, are my parent, my friend, my knowledge, my wealth and my everything.
3. Prayer is practised with humility and respect. Mocking breaks the spirit of the prayer.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Mandirs in your county and in Kenya

LESSON 6: MANDIRS IN YOUR COUNTY AND IN KENYA
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Identify a Hindu mandir in their own locality or the nearest one they can find on a map.
• Record its name and place without inventing details.

Curriculum outcomes: d) identify the Hindu places of worship in their locality for familiarisation; e) map the Hindu Mandir (temples) in Kenya for exact location

## Introduction
A mandir is a Sanatan or Hindu temple, a building set apart for darshan, prayer and community. Kenya has mandirs where Hindu families live. Your task is to find a real one, not to guess a name.

## Notes
### What a mandir is for
People go to a mandir to see the murti, to pray, to hear bhajan and aarti, to celebrate festivals and to meet as a community. A mandir is a place of worship, so behaviour there is quieter and more careful than in a market. Shoes come off. Voices drop.

### In your locality
Start with what is near you. Ask a parent, a teacher or a family friend whether there is a Sanatan or Hindu mandir in your estate, town or county. Write the name they give you. If you have visited it, describe only what you really saw: a gate, a hall, a dome or tower, a courtyard. If you have not visited it, do not pretend you have.

If there is no mandir in your county, say so honestly. Then look for the nearest one in a neighbouring county. 'Nearest' must come from an adult or from a map, not from imagination.

### Mapping
Use a printed map of Kenya or a digital map with your teacher. Find your county. Mark the town where the mandir stands. Notice the direction from your home: towards the coast, towards the lake, or within your own town. Write the name of the mandir and the town. Do not invent a distance in kilometres. If the map shows a scale and your teacher helps you read it, you may record that distance. Otherwise write 'distance not measured'.

One mandir that many Kenyan learners see in photographs is the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir. It is a real Hindu mandir. It may not be the one nearest your school. Always name the mandir your map or your family actually identifies.

### A collage without fake labels
Pictures for a collage should be of real temples. Label a picture only when you know what it is. A photo of a building you cannot identify should be labelled 'mandir, name not yet known' until an adult helps you.

## Key words
• mandir — a Sanatan or Hindu temple
• locality — the area around your home or school
• darshan — seeing the murti with reverence

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class is asked for a mandir in their county. Nobody has visited one. What is an honest answer?

Working:
1. Do not invent a name or a street.
2. Ask a teacher or parent, or search a map together.
3. If none is in the county, record the nearest real mandir and say it is outside the county.

Answer: Find a real mandir with an adult or a map, or state clearly that the nearest one is outside the county.

## Activity: Map a mandir
You will need: A map of Kenya, A digital device if the teacher allows, Paper for a collage
1. With your teacher, locate your county on a map of Kenya.
2. Identify a Sanatan or Hindu mandir in your locality, or the nearest one an adult can confirm. Write its name and town.
3. Make a collage of mandir pictures. Label only the pictures you can name truthfully.
4. Share one fact you are sure of, and one question you still need to ask.

## Practice
1. What is a mandir?
2. How can you find the location of a mandir in Kenya without inventing it?
3. Why should a collage label be left blank if you do not know the mandir's name?

## Summary
• A mandir is a Hindu place of worship.
• Learners identify a real mandir near their home or on a map of Kenya.
• Unknown names and distances are left unknown rather than invented.

### Answers to practice
1. A Sanatan or Hindu temple, used for prayer, darshan and community worship.
2. Ask a parent or teacher, or use a map or search with an adult, and write only what you can confirm.
3. A wrong label teaches a false fact. It is better to say the name is not yet known.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Rites and rituals in a mandir

LESSON 7: RITES AND RITUALS IN A MANDIR
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Describe the rites a visitor should observe in a Sanatan or Hindu mandir.
• Explain why those rites are kept.

Curriculum outcomes: f) observe rites and rituals while visiting Sanatan/Hindu Mandirs in Kenya (temple)

## Introduction
Walking into a mandir as if it were a shop confuses everyone and can offend the worshippers. Rites and rituals are the agreed ways of showing respect. They also help the mind slow down.

## Notes
### Before you enter
Go with a parent, a teacher or the school. Dress neatly and modestly. Leave shoes on the rack provided. Some mandirs ask you to wash your hands or feet. Switch a phone to silent. Do not chew gum or eat snacks as you walk in.

### Inside
- Bow when you come before the murti. You may join your hands in namaskara.
- Do not touch the murti unless a priest invites that action. In most visits, looking with respect is the right darshan.
- If you are offered a plate to make an offering, follow the family's custom: a flower, a little water or incense may be used. Do not invent a rite.
- Sit on the floor if that is the custom, without pointing your feet rudely at the shrine.
- Join the aarti quietly if it is happening. Move your hands only as your host shows you. Receive prasad in your right hand, or as you are shown, and do not snatch.
- Walk around the shrine only if that pradakshina is part of the visit and you are shown the direction. In many mandirs people keep the shrine on their right.
- Speak softly. Children do not run between worshippers.

### Why these rites exist
They show that the place and the murti are honoured. They protect holy objects from careless handling. They give every person, including a stranger, the same pattern so that nobody has to guess. A ritual repeated with attention becomes prayer in the body, not an empty habit.

### After the visit
Thank the host. Write what you actually observed. If a rite was new, ask its name. Do not photograph people or the inner shrine if the mandir asks you not to.

## Key words
• rite — a set religious action
• aarti — a ritual of waving a lamp before the murti while prayers are sung
• prasad — food or a gift received as a blessing after worship

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During aarti a visitor starts a loud video call. What should they have done, and why?

Working:
1. Aarti is a rite of worship and needs quiet attention.
2. The phone should have been silent and put away.
3. The visitor can step outside if a call is urgent, then return quietly.

Answer: Keep the phone silent and put it away so that the aarti is not disturbed.

## Activity: Prepare for a mandir visit
You will need: A checklist, Permission from families if a visit is planned
1. With the teacher, make a checklist: modest dress, shoes off, quiet voice, no touching the murti, phone silent, receive prasad politely.
2. If a visit is possible, observe the rites and the important features with the host. If a visit is not possible, practise the checklist in a role-play.
3. Write three rites you must observe and one reason rites matter.
4. Include every classmate in the role-play, offering a seated role to anyone who needs it.

## Practice
1. Name three rites or manners to observe when visiting a mandir.
2. What is aarti?
3. Why are rites observed in a mandir?

## Summary
• Visitors remove shoes, speak softly, bow, and do not touch the murti unless invited.
• Aarti and prasad are received with attention.
• Rites show honour and help everyone share one respectful pattern.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: remove shoes, dress modestly, speak softly, bow, do not touch the murti, silence the phone, receive prasad politely.
2. A ritual in which a lamp is waved before the murti while prayers are offered.
3. They show respect for the murti and the place, protect holy objects, and help worshippers act in one reverent way.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: The beauty of the mandir

LESSON 8: THE BEAUTY OF THE MANDIR
==================================

## What you will learn
• Describe common architectural features of a Hindu mandir.
• Explain how careful building shows honour and welcome.

Curriculum outcomes: f) observe rites and rituals while visiting Sanatan/Hindu Mandirs in Kenya (temple); g) appreciate the architecture of the place of worship for developing a sense of aesthetics

## Introduction
A mandir is not only a hall with a roof. Towers, carvings, lamps and a clear path to the shrine are there for a reason. Looking closely is part of appreciating the place of worship.

## Notes
### Features to notice
Mandirs are not all identical. As you look at a picture or a real building, watch for these parts:
- **Garbhagriha** — the inner shrine where the main murti rests. It is the heart of the temple.
- **Shikhara or dome** — a tower or rounded roof that makes the shrine visible from far away and lifts the eye upward.
- **Mandapa** — a hall or porch where people sit, sing and listen.
- **Gateway and courtyard** — the entrance that takes you from the busy street into a calmer space. Shoes are left near here.
- **Carvings and colour** — figures from scripture, flowers and patterns cut in stone or wood, or painted on walls. They teach stories to people who may not be reading at that moment.
- **Lamps and bells** — light and sound used in worship.

You may not see every feature in every Kenyan mandir. Some communities worship in a simple hall. Simplicity can be beautiful too. Describe what is there.

### Why beauty belongs to worship
Careful architecture says that Paramatma is worthy of our best skill. A clean floor, a straight row of lamps and a protected shrine help worshippers feel safe and attentive. A sense of aesthetics means you notice what is well made and you do not spoil it with litter, scribbles or rough play.

### Draw what you understand
When you draw a mandir, include a shrine and a place for people to sit, and leave shoes outside the door in the picture. Colour calmly. If you add a tower, you may label it shikhara. Do not copy a classmate's drawing and hand it in as yours.

On a visit, notice one feature you find beautiful and one rule you kept. Both belong to respect: the eye learns, and the body behaves.

## Key words
• garbhagriha — the inner shrine of a mandir
• shikhara — the tower rising above the shrine
• aesthetics — a sense of what is beautiful and well made

## Activity: Draw and colour a mandir
You will need: Paper, Colour pencils, Pictures of mandirs
1. Look at pictures of Sanatan or Hindu mandirs, including any you have mapped in Kenya.
2. Draw a mandir with a shrine entrance, a hall and a tower or dome. Add a shoe rack outside.
3. Label at least two features, such as shikhara and mandapa.
4. Write two sentences: one about a rite a visitor must observe, and one about a feature you find beautiful.

## Practice
1. What is the garbhagriha?
2. What is a shikhara?
3. Why does the architecture of a mandir matter?

## Summary
• A mandir may have a garbhagriha, a shikhara or dome, a mandapa and a courtyard.
• Not every mandir looks the same. Describe the one you actually see.
• Beautiful work and careful rites both show honour.

### Answers to practice
1. The inner shrine where the main murti is kept.
2. The tower that rises above the shrine.
3. It honours God, teaches through carvings and shape, and helps worshippers feel attentive and welcome.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Dainik Prarthana means daily prayer. This sub-strand teaches three Sanatan prayers: the Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey, and Saraswati Vandana. You will learn when each is recited, what the words mean, and how to behave in a Hindu mandir, including mandirs in Kenya.

## Strand 4.0: Worship
Sub-strand 4.1: Dainik Prarthana (Daily prayers)
Suggested lessons: 10

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation
b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith
c) appreciate the importance of prayers in daily life for spiritual development
d) identify the Hindu places of worship in their locality for familiarisation
e) map the Hindu Mandir (temples) in Kenya for exact location
f) observe rites and rituals while visiting Sanatan/Hindu Mandirs in Kenya (temple)
g) appreciate the architecture of the place of worship for developing a sense of aesthetics

## What this sub-strand covers
• Gayatri Mantra
• Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey
• Saraswati Vandana

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why are prayers important in our daily life?
2. What is the significance of reciting prayers at different times?
3. Why are rites and rituals observed in a Sanatan/Hindu Mandir?

## Core competencies
• Communication: Learner develops speaking skills during practice of reciting prayers with peers.
• Digital Literacy: Learner interacts with technology by using search engines for enhancing information about Sanatan/Hindu Mandir.

## Values
• Respect: Learner inculcates humility during practice of reciting prayers with peers.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Citizenship: Learner enhances social cohesion when visiting Sanatan/Hindu Mandir (temple) to witness the rites and rituals, architecture and important features of the Sanatan/Hindu Mandir (temple).

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link the skill of applying geographical knowledge and using digital devices to map the Sanatan/Hindu Mandir (temple) in Kenya to skills learnt in Social Studies.
• Learner is able to link skills of making collage of pictures of temples in their locality a draw and colour the Sanatan/Hindu Mandir (temple) to the creative skills learnt in Creative Arts.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 4.0 Worship, Sub-strand 4.1 Dainik Prarthana (Daily prayers)

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Why daily prayer matters
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: WHY DAILY PRAYER MATTERS
==================================

## What you will learn
• Explain why prayer is part of a day, not only of a festival.
• Name the three prayers to be learned and a time that fits each one.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; c) appreciate the importance of prayers in daily life for spiritual development

## Introduction
Some people only fold their hands when they are afraid. Daily prayer is steadier than that. It is a way of beginning the morning, starting study, or ending worship by remembering God on purpose.

## Notes
### What prayer is
Prayer is speaking with Paramatma. It can be thanks, praise, a request for a clean mind, or a promise to do what is right. In Sanatan life, set prayers are learned by heart so that the mouth and the mind can rest on true words instead of rushing into the day.

Daily prayer does not replace kindness. A learner who chants and then cheats has missed the point. Prayer is meant to make the rest of the day more honest, more attentive and less selfish. That is spiritual development: a slow growth in love of God and in good character.

### Three prayers, different moments
This sub-strand names three prayers, all from Sanatan or Hindu tradition:
- **Gayatri Mantra** — a morning and worship prayer asking the divine light to guide the mind
- **Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey** — a prayer of trust, often near the close of worship, saying that God is mother, father, friend and everything
- **Saraswati Vandana** — a salutation to Saraswati before study, asking for true learning

Knowing which prayer fits which occasion is part of familiarisation. You would not treat a prayer before study as a joke at the back of the class, and you would not rush the Gayatri while pushing in a queue.

### Times of day
Morning prayer sets the mind before work. A prayer before lessons asks for understanding rather than for an easy way to avoid work. An evening or closing prayer hands the day back to God, including the parts that went badly. Festivals have extra prayers, but these three are for ordinary days.

Recite only the words you have been taught carefully. Do not invent extra lines. Listen to a correct recording if your teacher provides one, and match the sound with respect.

## Key words
• dainik — daily
• prarthana — prayer
• familiarisation — getting to know something so that it is no longer strange

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which prayer fits the start of a study period: Saraswati Vandana, a made-up rhyme, or a joke about a classmate?

Working:
1. Saraswati is honoured as the deity of learning.
2. Saraswati Vandana is the prayer this sub-strand links with study.
3. A joke is not a prayer.

Answer: Saraswati Vandana.

## Activity: Prayers and occasions
You will need: Three cards, A resource person or teacher
1. Listen as a resource person or teacher names the three prayers and one occasion for each.
2. Label the cards Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey and Saraswati Vandana.
3. Under each title write the occasion: guiding the mind, trusting God as parent and friend, or beginning study.
4. Say why a daily prayer can help a learner more than praying only in a panic.

## Practice
1. What does Dainik Prarthana mean?
2. Name the three prayers in this sub-strand.
3. Why is prayer before an examination not a substitute for revision?

## Summary
• Daily prayer remembers God and steadies the day.
• The three prayers are the Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey and Saraswati Vandana.
• Each prayer has a fitting time.

### Answers to practice
1. Daily prayer.
2. Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey and Saraswati Vandana.
3. Prayer asks for a clear and honest mind. The learner still needs to study.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: The Gayatri Mantra
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: THE GAYATRI MANTRA
============================

## What you will learn
• Recite the Gayatri Mantra correctly and calmly.
• Explain its meaning in simple English.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith

## Introduction
The Gayatri Mantra is a very old Vedic prayer to the divine light that gives understanding. Many Sanatan families recite it in the morning. You will learn the words slowly, then the meaning, so that the mouth does not run ahead of the mind.

## Notes
### The words
Learn this form, line by line:

Om bhur bhuvah svah
Tat savitur varenyam
Bhargo devasya dhimahi
Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat

Say it softly at first. Keep the ends of the words clear. Do not turn it into a race. If a line is difficult, your teacher or a recording can give the sound. Intonation means the rise and fall of the voice. A respectful tone is steady, not shouted and not giggled.

### The meaning
In simple English the prayer says: we meditate on the excellent glory of the Creator, the divine light. May that light inspire and guide our understanding.

Bhur, bhuvah and svah name the earth, the middle space and the heaven, a way of saying the whole world. Savitur points to the divine source of light. The last line is the request: may our thoughts be led in the right direction.

### When it is used
The Gayatri is recited in the morning, at sandhya time in homes that keep that custom, and during many acts of worship. At school it may be recited at assembly when the teacher has chosen it. It is a prayer for wisdom, so it also fits a quiet moment before study. It is not a spell for winning by cheating.

### How to practise
Stand or sit straight. Hands may be joined. Breathe in, then recite without straining the throat. Learn one line a day if you need to. When you can say all four lines, add the meaning in your own words so that faith and understanding stay together.

All learners in the class may learn this prayer as part of the lesson. Reciting it is a way of understanding Sanatan worship. Join with respect, even if your family also has other prayers at home.

## Key words
• Gayatri Mantra — a Vedic prayer asking divine light to guide the mind
• intonation — the musical rise and fall of the voice when reciting

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner can say the Gayatri quickly but cannot explain it. What should they add?

Working:
1. Correct sound matters, but the outcome also asks for meaning.
2. They should be able to say that the prayer meditates on divine light and asks that light to guide the mind.
3. Speed without meaning is not enough.

Answer: They should learn the simple meaning and recite more calmly.

## Activity: Practise the Gayatri with a partner
You will need: The four lines written clearly by the teacher, An audio recording if one is available
1. Listen to the teacher or to a recording of the Gayatri Mantra.
2. Repeat one line at a time with a partner, then say all four lines together.
3. Tell your partner the meaning in your own words.
4. Encourage a classmate who needs a slower pace. Do not laugh at a mistake; model the line again.

## Practice
1. Write the four lines of the Gayatri Mantra you were taught.
2. What does the Gayatri ask for?
3. Name one fitting time to recite the Gayatri.

## Summary
• The Gayatri asks divine light to guide our understanding.
• It is recited in the morning and in worship, calmly and clearly.
• Meaning and correct words belong together.

### Answers to practice
1. Om bhur bhuvah svah. Tat savitur varenyam. Bhargo devasya dhimahi. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat.
2. That the divine light of the Creator will guide and inspire our minds.
3. In the morning, during worship, or quietly before study.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: TWAMEV MATA CHA PITA TWAMEY
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Recite Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey.
• Explain that the prayer calls God mother, father, friend and everything.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith

## Introduction
Children know what it is to need a parent or a friend. This prayer says that God is all of those, and more. It is a prayer of trust, often sung or spoken near the end of worship.

## Notes
### The words
The name on the design is Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey. The prayer is learned in these four lines:

Twameva mata cha pita twameva
Twameva bandhush cha sakha twameva
Twameva vidya dravinam twameva
Twameva sarvam mama deva deva

Twameva means 'you alone'. Speak the lines evenly. The sound 'cha' is 'and'. Do not skip the third line, which is easy to forget.

### The meaning
- You alone are my mother, and you alone are my father.
- You alone are my relative, and you alone are my friend.
- You alone are my knowledge, and you alone are my wealth.
- You alone are my everything, O God of gods.

The prayer does not tell you to ignore your human parents. It says that behind every good gift, including parents, friends and learning, is Paramatma. When a parent is far away, or a friend disappoints you, the prayer is a place to rest trust.

### When it is used
Many congregations recite it at the close of puja or aarti, when worshippers offer the whole day to God. It can also be a personal evening prayer. It is a prayer of belonging, not a prayer for showing off a loud voice.

### A meaning to keep
If God is your mother and father, then you are not abandoned. If God is your wealth, then cheating to get money is a strange answer to the prayer. If God is your knowledge, then learning is received with thanks, not with pride that insults slower learners.

Practise until you can recite it without the card, then say the meaning once in English.

## Key words
• twameva — you alone
• sakha — friend
• vidya — knowledge or learning

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which line means that God is mother and father, and which line means that God is knowledge and wealth?

Working:
1. Mata means mother and pita means father: the first line.
2. Vidya means knowledge and dravinam means wealth: the third line.
3. The second line is relative and friend. The fourth line says God is everything.

Answer: The first line is mother and father. The third line is knowledge and wealth.

## Activity: Recite and explain Twameva
You will need: The four lines on the board, Exercise book
1. Listen to the prayer from the teacher or an audio device.
2. Practise with a peer until both of you can say the four lines.
3. Write the English meaning of each line.
4. One pair recites during a class assembly or a class prayer time if the teacher invites you. Help a classmate who needs the lines pointed to as you say them.

## Practice
1. Recite the four lines of Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey.
2. What does the first line mean?
3. When is this prayer often recited?

## Summary
• Twameva says that God alone is mother, father, relative, friend, knowledge, wealth and everything.
• It is often recited at the close of worship.
• Trust in God should make us more grateful, not proud or dishonest.

### Answers to practice
1. Twameva mata cha pita twameva. Twameva bandhush cha sakha twameva. Twameva vidya dravinam twameva. Twameva sarvam mama deva deva.
2. You alone are my mother and you alone are my father.
3. At the close of puja or aarti, and as a prayer of trust.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Saraswati Vandana
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: SARASWATI VANDANA
===========================

## What you will learn
• Recite the Saraswati Vandana used in this lesson.
• Explain who Saraswati is and why the prayer is said before study.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith

## Introduction
Before a music lesson or a page of reading, some learners simply start. A Sanatan prayer before study does something more. It greets Saraswati, the deity of knowledge, speech and the arts, and asks that learning be successful and clean.

## Notes
### Who Saraswati is
In Sanatan tradition Saraswati is the deity of learning, speech, music and wisdom. She is often shown in white, seated with a veena and a book, and with a swan nearby. White suggests a clear mind. The book suggests study. You do not need a picture in order to pray, but a picture can help you remember who is being greeted. A vandana is a salutation, a respectful greeting.

### The words to learn
This is the short vandana used before study:

Saraswati namastubhyam
Varade kamarupini
Vidyarambham karishyami
Siddhir bhavatu me sada

Namastubhyam means 'I bow to you'. Vidyarambham karishyami means 'I am about to begin my learning'. Siddhir bhavatu me sada means 'May success always be mine'.

The whole prayer says: O Saraswati, I bow to you, giver of blessings, who grants what is rightly wished. I am beginning my study. May I always succeed.

### Success of the right kind
Success here does not mean passing by copying. It means understanding, remembering and using knowledge well. A learner may recite this vandana at assembly, at the start of homework, or before a school performance of music or reading. Recite it, then do the work.

### Practice
Join your hands, recite slowly, and then open your book. If you forget a line, begin again rather than mumbling. Peers can test each other kindly: one says the first line, the other says the second, and then you swap.

## Key words
• Saraswati — the Sanatan deity of learning, speech and the arts
• vandana — a salutation or prayer of respectful greeting
• vidya — knowledge or learning

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A class wants a prayer for the moment they open their exercise books. Which of the three prayers fits best, and why?

Working:
1. The Gayatri asks for a guided mind and can also be used in the morning.
2. Twameva is especially a prayer of trust at the close of worship.
3. Saraswati Vandana directly says, 'I am beginning my learning.'

Answer: Saraswati Vandana, because it is a salutation before study.

## Activity: Saraswati Vandana before a short reading
You will need: The four lines on a chart, A paragraph of any school reading
1. Listen to the vandana and repeat each line.
2. Say the meaning together: I bow to Saraswati; I am beginning my learning; may I succeed.
3. Recite the prayer, then read one paragraph silently and tell a partner one fact you understood.
4. Invite a learner who speaks softly to recite with the group so that nobody is left out.

## Practice
1. Recite the Saraswati Vandana taught in this lesson.
2. Who is Saraswati?
3. What does 'Vidyarambham karishyami' mean?

## Summary
• Saraswati is the deity of learning.
• The vandana bows to her and asks for success as study begins.
• Real success includes honest work after the prayer.

### Answers to practice
1. Saraswati namastubhyam. Varade kamarupini. Vidyarambham karishyami. Siddhir bhavatu me sada.
2. The Sanatan deity of learning, speech, music and wisdom.
3. I am beginning my learning.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Reciting at the right time
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: RECITING AT THE RIGHT TIME
====================================

## What you will learn
• Match each prayer to its occasion.
• Recite all three prayers with respect for classmates.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the three selected prayers performed for different occasions for familiarisation; b) recite the three selected prayers for understanding the meanings to deepen the faith; c) appreciate the importance of prayers in daily life for spiritual development

## Introduction
A tool used at the wrong time can still be a good tool. Prayer is similar. The words of the Gayatri, Twameva and the Saraswati Vandana are all valuable, and each one has a moment when its meaning is especially clear.

## Notes
### A simple guide
- Recite the **Gayatri Mantra** when you are beginning the day or joining worship and you want your mind led by divine light.
- Recite **Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey** when worship is closing or when you need to remember that God holds you as parent and friend.
- Recite **Saraswati Vandana** when you open a book, begin a lesson, or start music and art practice.

Nothing stops a family from using a prayer at another sincere moment. This guide stops the three from being jumbled in your memory.

### Why timing matters
Words sink in when they match the action. Saying 'I am beginning my learning' and then chatting for twenty minutes wastes the prayer. Saying 'you alone are my wealth' and then stealing a coin from a bag is a contradiction. The significance of time is that the body is about to do something, and the prayer points that action towards God.

### Manners while others recite
Stand still in assembly. If you are not reciting, keep silent rather than mocking the sound. Humility means you do not shove a partner who is slower. Offer the first line quietly if they ask for help. Correct intonation comes from listening, not from shouting over the group.

### A week's plan
Morning: Gayatri, even two careful repetitions. Before homework: Saraswati Vandana. After a family or class prayer: Twameva. At the end of the week, notice whether the prayers changed anything small: less panic, a kinder reply, or homework actually started.

Spiritual development is that noticing. The prayers are short enough for a child. Their meanings are large enough for a lifetime.

## Key words
• occasion — the time or event for which something is used
• humility — a modest spirit that does not put you above others

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Match the prayers to these moments: opening a mathematics book, morning assembly, the end of aarti.

Working:
1. Opening a book matches Saraswati Vandana.
2. Morning assembly matches the Gayatri Mantra.
3. The end of aarti matches Twameva.

Answer: Saraswati Vandana; Gayatri Mantra; Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey.

## Activity: Assembly practice
You will need: The three prayers written out, A quiet space
1. In pairs, recite each prayer once and say its occasion before you begin.
2. Listen to an audio recording if the teacher has one, and copy the calm pace.
3. As a class, recite one prayer as you would at assembly. Stand straight and wait for the signal to start.
4. Afterwards, tell your partner one reason daily prayer helps spiritual growth. Encourage a classmate who is still learning the lines.

## Practice
1. Which prayer is the best match for the start of homework, and why?
2. Give the meaning of Twameva in one sentence.
3. Why should you not mock a classmate who recites slowly?

## Summary
• Gayatri for morning and a guided mind, Saraswati Vandana before study, Twameva at the close of worship.
• The prayer should match the action that follows.
• Classmates recite together with humility.

### Answers to practice
1. Saraswati Vandana, because it greets the deity of learning as study begins.
2. You alone, O God, are my parent, my friend, my knowledge, my wealth and my everything.
3. Prayer is practised with humility and respect. Mocking breaks the spirit of the prayer.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Mandirs in your county and in Kenya
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: MANDIRS IN YOUR COUNTY AND IN KENYA
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Identify a Hindu mandir in their own locality or the nearest one they can find on a map.
• Record its name and place without inventing details.

Curriculum outcomes: d) identify the Hindu places of worship in their locality for familiarisation; e) map the Hindu Mandir (temples) in Kenya for exact location

## Introduction
A mandir is a Sanatan or Hindu temple, a building set apart for darshan, prayer and community. Kenya has mandirs where Hindu families live. Your task is to find a real one, not to guess a name.

## Notes
### What a mandir is for
People go to a mandir to see the murti, to pray, to hear bhajan and aarti, to celebrate festivals and to meet as a community. A mandir is a place of worship, so behaviour there is quieter and more careful than in a market. Shoes come off. Voices drop.

### In your locality
Start with what is near you. Ask a parent, a teacher or a family friend whether there is a Sanatan or Hindu mandir in your estate, town or county. Write the name they give you. If you have visited it, describe only what you really saw: a gate, a hall, a dome or tower, a courtyard. If you have not visited it, do not pretend you have.

If there is no mandir in your county, say so honestly. Then look for the nearest one in a neighbouring county. 'Nearest' must come from an adult or from a map, not from imagination.

### Mapping
Use a printed map of Kenya or a digital map with your teacher. Find your county. Mark the town where the mandir stands. Notice the direction from your home: towards the coast, towards the lake, or within your own town. Write the name of the mandir and the town. Do not invent a distance in kilometres. If the map shows a scale and your teacher helps you read it, you may record that distance. Otherwise write 'distance not measured'.

One mandir that many Kenyan learners see in photographs is the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir. It is a real Hindu mandir. It may not be the one nearest your school. Always name the mandir your map or your family actually identifies.

### A collage without fake labels
Pictures for a collage should be of real temples. Label a picture only when you know what it is. A photo of a building you cannot identify should be labelled 'mandir, name not yet known' until an adult helps you.

## Key words
• mandir — a Sanatan or Hindu temple
• locality — the area around your home or school
• darshan — seeing the murti with reverence

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class is asked for a mandir in their county. Nobody has visited one. What is an honest answer?

Working:
1. Do not invent a name or a street.
2. Ask a teacher or parent, or search a map together.
3. If none is in the county, record the nearest real mandir and say it is outside the county.

Answer: Find a real mandir with an adult or a map, or state clearly that the nearest one is outside the county.

## Activity: Map a mandir
You will need: A map of Kenya, A digital device if the teacher allows, Paper for a collage
1. With your teacher, locate your county on a map of Kenya.
2. Identify a Sanatan or Hindu mandir in your locality, or the nearest one an adult can confirm. Write its name and town.
3. Make a collage of mandir pictures. Label only the pictures you can name truthfully.
4. Share one fact you are sure of, and one question you still need to ask.

## Practice
1. What is a mandir?
2. How can you find the location of a mandir in Kenya without inventing it?
3. Why should a collage label be left blank if you do not know the mandir's name?

## Summary
• A mandir is a Hindu place of worship.
• Learners identify a real mandir near their home or on a map of Kenya.
• Unknown names and distances are left unknown rather than invented.

### Answers to practice
1. A Sanatan or Hindu temple, used for prayer, darshan and community worship.
2. Ask a parent or teacher, or use a map or search with an adult, and write only what you can confirm.
3. A wrong label teaches a false fact. It is better to say the name is not yet known.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Rites and rituals in a mandir
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: RITES AND RITUALS IN A MANDIR
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Describe the rites a visitor should observe in a Sanatan or Hindu mandir.
• Explain why those rites are kept.

Curriculum outcomes: f) observe rites and rituals while visiting Sanatan/Hindu Mandirs in Kenya (temple)

## Introduction
Walking into a mandir as if it were a shop confuses everyone and can offend the worshippers. Rites and rituals are the agreed ways of showing respect. They also help the mind slow down.

## Notes
### Before you enter
Go with a parent, a teacher or the school. Dress neatly and modestly. Leave shoes on the rack provided. Some mandirs ask you to wash your hands or feet. Switch a phone to silent. Do not chew gum or eat snacks as you walk in.

### Inside
- Bow when you come before the murti. You may join your hands in namaskara.
- Do not touch the murti unless a priest invites that action. In most visits, looking with respect is the right darshan.
- If you are offered a plate to make an offering, follow the family's custom: a flower, a little water or incense may be used. Do not invent a rite.
- Sit on the floor if that is the custom, without pointing your feet rudely at the shrine.
- Join the aarti quietly if it is happening. Move your hands only as your host shows you. Receive prasad in your right hand, or as you are shown, and do not snatch.
- Walk around the shrine only if that pradakshina is part of the visit and you are shown the direction. In many mandirs people keep the shrine on their right.
- Speak softly. Children do not run between worshippers.

### Why these rites exist
They show that the place and the murti are honoured. They protect holy objects from careless handling. They give every person, including a stranger, the same pattern so that nobody has to guess. A ritual repeated with attention becomes prayer in the body, not an empty habit.

### After the visit
Thank the host. Write what you actually observed. If a rite was new, ask its name. Do not photograph people or the inner shrine if the mandir asks you not to.

## Key words
• rite — a set religious action
• aarti — a ritual of waving a lamp before the murti while prayers are sung
• prasad — food or a gift received as a blessing after worship

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During aarti a visitor starts a loud video call. What should they have done, and why?

Working:
1. Aarti is a rite of worship and needs quiet attention.
2. The phone should have been silent and put away.
3. The visitor can step outside if a call is urgent, then return quietly.

Answer: Keep the phone silent and put it away so that the aarti is not disturbed.

## Activity: Prepare for a mandir visit
You will need: A checklist, Permission from families if a visit is planned
1. With the teacher, make a checklist: modest dress, shoes off, quiet voice, no touching the murti, phone silent, receive prasad politely.
2. If a visit is possible, observe the rites and the important features with the host. If a visit is not possible, practise the checklist in a role-play.
3. Write three rites you must observe and one reason rites matter.
4. Include every classmate in the role-play, offering a seated role to anyone who needs it.

## Practice
1. Name three rites or manners to observe when visiting a mandir.
2. What is aarti?
3. Why are rites observed in a mandir?

## Summary
• Visitors remove shoes, speak softly, bow, and do not touch the murti unless invited.
• Aarti and prasad are received with attention.
• Rites show honour and help everyone share one respectful pattern.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: remove shoes, dress modestly, speak softly, bow, do not touch the murti, silence the phone, receive prasad politely.
2. A ritual in which a lamp is waved before the murti while prayers are offered.
3. They show respect for the murti and the place, protect holy objects, and help worshippers act in one reverent way.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: The beauty of the mandir
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: THE BEAUTY OF THE MANDIR
==================================

## What you will learn
• Describe common architectural features of a Hindu mandir.
• Explain how careful building shows honour and welcome.

Curriculum outcomes: f) observe rites and rituals while visiting Sanatan/Hindu Mandirs in Kenya (temple); g) appreciate the architecture of the place of worship for developing a sense of aesthetics

## Introduction
A mandir is not only a hall with a roof. Towers, carvings, lamps and a clear path to the shrine are there for a reason. Looking closely is part of appreciating the place of worship.

## Notes
### Features to notice
Mandirs are not all identical. As you look at a picture or a real building, watch for these parts:
- **Garbhagriha** — the inner shrine where the main murti rests. It is the heart of the temple.
- **Shikhara or dome** — a tower or rounded roof that makes the shrine visible from far away and lifts the eye upward.
- **Mandapa** — a hall or porch where people sit, sing and listen.
- **Gateway and courtyard** — the entrance that takes you from the busy street into a calmer space. Shoes are left near here.
- **Carvings and colour** — figures from scripture, flowers and patterns cut in stone or wood, or painted on walls. They teach stories to people who may not be reading at that moment.
- **Lamps and bells** — light and sound used in worship.

You may not see every feature in every Kenyan mandir. Some communities worship in a simple hall. Simplicity can be beautiful too. Describe what is there.

### Why beauty belongs to worship
Careful architecture says that Paramatma is worthy of our best skill. A clean floor, a straight row of lamps and a protected shrine help worshippers feel safe and attentive. A sense of aesthetics means you notice what is well made and you do not spoil it with litter, scribbles or rough play.

### Draw what you understand
When you draw a mandir, include a shrine and a place for people to sit, and leave shoes outside the door in the picture. Colour calmly. If you add a tower, you may label it shikhara. Do not copy a classmate's drawing and hand it in as yours.

On a visit, notice one feature you find beautiful and one rule you kept. Both belong to respect: the eye learns, and the body behaves.

## Key words
• garbhagriha — the inner shrine of a mandir
• shikhara — the tower rising above the shrine
• aesthetics — a sense of what is beautiful and well made

## Activity: Draw and colour a mandir
You will need: Paper, Colour pencils, Pictures of mandirs
1. Look at pictures of Sanatan or Hindu mandirs, including any you have mapped in Kenya.
2. Draw a mandir with a shrine entrance, a hall and a tower or dome. Add a shoe rack outside.
3. Label at least two features, such as shikhara and mandapa.
4. Write two sentences: one about a rite a visitor must observe, and one about a feature you find beautiful.

## Practice
1. What is the garbhagriha?
2. What is a shikhara?
3. Why does the architecture of a mandir matter?

## Summary
• A mandir may have a garbhagriha, a shikhara or dome, a mandapa and a courtyard.
• Not every mandir looks the same. Describe the one you actually see.
• Beautiful work and careful rites both show honour.

### Answers to practice
1. The inner shrine where the main murti is kept.
2. The tower that rises above the shrine.
3. It honours God, teaches through carvings and shape, and helps worshippers feel attentive and welcome.

questions.question: Which three prayers does this sub-strand teach?
options: Gayatri Mantra, Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey, Saraswati Vandana
questions.explanation: The design names these three Sanatan daily prayers.

questions.question: The Gayatri Mantra asks that
options: Divine light will guide our understanding
A mandir will be built in one day
Shoes will be worn inside the shrine
questions.explanation: The mantra meditates on the Creator's light and asks it to inspire the mind.

questions.question: Which line begins the prayer Twamev Mata cha Pita Twamey?
questions.explanation: That line means 'You alone are my mother and you alone are my father.'

questions.question: Saraswati Vandana is most fitting
options: As a joke in the playground
Before study, because Saraswati is the deity of learning
Only while running in the corridor
As a replacement for telling the truth
questions.explanation: The vandana greets Saraswati as learning begins.

questions.question: Why are daily prayers important?
options: They help a person remember God and grow spiritually through the ordinary day
questions.explanation: Prayer supports spiritual development when it is joined to good conduct.

questions.question: A mandir is
options: A Sanatan or Hindu place of worship
questions.explanation: Mandir is the word for a Hindu temple.

questions.question: How should learners map mandirs in Kenya?
questions.answer: They should use a map or an adult's help and record a real mandir's name and town, without inventing a place.
questions.explanation: The location must be exact and truthful.

questions.question: Which action observes mandir rites correctly?
options: Keep shoes on and touch every murti
Remove shoes, speak softly and do not touch the murti unless invited
Start a loud video during aarti
questions.explanation: These are basic rites of respect in a Sanatan mandir.

questions.question: The inner shrine of a mandir is called the
questions.explanation: Garbhagriha is the innermost sanctuary where the main murti rests.

questions.question: What is a shikhara, and why is it part of the beauty of a mandir?
questions.answer: It is the tower above the shrine. It lifts the building upward and helps worshippers see that the place is set apart for God.
questions.explanation: Architecture is appreciated as a way of honouring the sacred.
